title: Book Eight (1811 - 12) — Chapter 1
paragraphs: After Prince Andrew's engagement to Natasha, Pierre suddenly felt — without any apparent reason — that it was impossible to go on living as before. Firmly convinced as he was of the truths revealed to him by his benefactor, and happy as he had been in perfecting his inner self, to which he had devoted himself with such passion — all the meaning of such a life vanished after Andrew's engagement and the death of Joseph Alexeevich, the news of which reached him almost simultaneously. Only the skeleton of life remained: his house, a brilliant wife who now enjoyed the favors of a very important personage, acquaintance with all of Petersburg, and his court service with its dull formalities. And this life suddenly seemed unbearably loathsome to Pierre. He stopped keeping a diary, avoided the Brothers, began going to the club again, drank heavily, and fell back in with the bachelor crowd, leading such a life that Countess Helene thought it necessary to scold him severely about it. Pierre felt she was right, and to avoid embarrassing her he left for Moscow.

In Moscow, as soon as he entered his huge house where the faded and aging princesses still lived with their enormous household; as soon as he drove through the city and saw the Iberian shrine with its countless candles burning before the golden icon covers, the Kremlin Square with its undisturbed snow, the cabbies and hovels of the Sivtsev Vrazhok — those old Muscovites who wanted nothing, hurried nowhere, and were peacefully living out their days; when he saw the old Moscow ladies, the Moscow balls, and the English Club — he felt himself at home in a quiet haven. In Moscow he felt at peace, at home, warm and slovenly as in an old dressing gown.

Moscow society, from the grandmothers down to the children, received Pierre like a long-awaited guest whose place was always ready and waiting. For Moscow society Pierre was the nicest, kindest, smartest, jolliest, and most generous of eccentrics — a heedless, good-natured nobleman of the old Russian type. His purse was always empty because it was open to everyone.

Benefit concerts, bad paintings, statues, charitable societies, gypsy choirs, schools, subscription dinners, drinking bouts, Freemasons, churches, and books — nothing and no one ever met with a refusal from him, and if it hadn't been for two friends who had borrowed large sums and taken him under their wing, he would have given everything away. There was never a dinner or soiree at the club without him. As soon as he sank into his spot on the sofa after two bottles of Margaux, people gathered around and the talking, arguing, and joking began. When quarrels broke out, his kindly smile and well-timed jokes reconciled the opponents. The Masonic dinners were dreary and dull when he wasn't there.

When, after a bachelor supper, he got up with his amiable, kindly smile and yielded to entreaties to go off somewhere with the revelers, shouts of delight and triumph arose among the young men. At balls he danced whenever a partner was needed. Young ladies, married and unmarried, liked him because he was equally friendly to all without making love to any of them, especially after supper. "He's charming; he has no sex," they said of him.
* "He is charming; he has no sex."
Pierre was one of those hundreds of retired gentlemen-in-waiting who were good-naturedly living out their days in Moscow.

How horrified he would have been seven years earlier, when he first came back from abroad, if someone had told him there was no need for him to seek or plan anything, that his groove had long been carved, predetermined from eternity, and that no matter how he wriggled he would become what everyone in his position became. He could not have believed it! Hadn't he once longed with all his heart to establish a republic in Russia; then to be a Napoleon; then a philosopher; then a strategist and the conqueror of Napoleon? Hadn't he seen the possibility of, and passionately desired, the regeneration of sinful humanity and his own rise to the highest perfection? Hadn't he established schools and hospitals and freed his serfs?

But instead of all that — here he was, the wealthy husband of an unfaithful wife, a retired gentleman-in-waiting, fond of eating and drinking and of — as he unbuttoned his waistcoat — grumbling about the government; a member of the Moscow English Club and a universal favorite in Moscow society. For a long time he couldn't reconcile himself to the idea that he had become one of those very same retired Moscow gentlemen-in-waiting he had so despised seven years ago.

Sometimes he consoled himself with the thought that he was only living this way temporarily; but then he was startled by the realization that how many others, like him, had entered this life and this club "temporarily" — with a full head of teeth and hair — and had only left when not a single tooth or hair remained.

In moments of pride, when he reflected on his position, it seemed to him that he was quite different from and distinct from those other retired gentlemen-in-waiting he had formerly looked down on: they were empty, stupid, self-satisfied fellows, content with their lot, "while I am still dissatisfied and want to do something for humanity. But perhaps all these comrades of mine struggled just as I did, looking for something new, a path of their own — and like me were brought by force of circumstances, of society, of upbringing, by that elemental force against which man is powerless, to the same state I'm in," he told himself in moments of humility. And after living in Moscow for a while he no longer despised but began to grow fond of, respect, and pity his fellows in fate, just as he pitied himself.

Pierre no longer suffered those acute bouts of despair, self-loathing, and disgust with life. But the same illness that had once expressed itself in those violent attacks was now driven inward and never left him for a moment. "What for? Why? What is going on in the world?" he would ask himself several times a day, perplexed, involuntarily starting to ponder the meaning of things anew. But knowing from experience that there were no answers to these questions, he quickly turned away from them and picked up a book, or hurried off to the club or to Apollon Nikolaevich's to swap the latest gossip.

"Helene, who has never cared about anything except her own body and is one of the stupidest women alive," thought Pierre, "is regarded by people as the pinnacle of intelligence and refinement, and they worship her. Napoleon Bonaparte was despised by everyone as long as he was great, but now that he has become a pathetic comedian, Emperor Francis wants to offer him his daughter in an illegal marriage. The Spaniards, through the Catholic clergy, offer thanks to God for their victory over the French on the fourteenth of June — and the French, also through the Catholic clergy, give thanks for defeating the Spaniards on that same fourteenth of June. My brother Masons swear by their blood that they are ready to sacrifice everything for their neighbor, but they won't give a ruble each to charity, and they scheme — the Astraea Lodge against the Manna Seekers — and fuss over an authentic Scottish carpet and a charter that nobody needs and whose very author doesn't understand. We all profess the Christian law of forgiving injuries and loving our neighbors — the law in whose honor we've built forty times forty churches in Moscow — but yesterday a deserter was flogged to death, and a minister of that same law of love and forgiveness gave the soldier a cross to kiss before his execution." So thought Pierre, and this whole universal deception — which everyone accepted, accustomed as they were to it — astonished him afresh each time, as if it were something new. "I see the deception and confusion," he thought, "but how am I to tell them all that I see? I have tried, and I've always found that they too, deep in their souls, understand it as I do — they just try not to look. So it seems this is how things must be! But I — what is to become of me?" he thought. He had the unfortunate capacity — common among men, especially Russians — of seeing and believing in the possibility of goodness and truth, but of seeing the evil and falsehood of life too clearly to be able to take any serious part in it. Every sphere of activity was connected, in his eyes, with evil and deception. Whatever he tried to be, whatever he took up, the evil and falsehood repelled him and blocked every path. Yet he had to live and find something to do. It was too terrible to exist under the burden of these unsolvable problems, so he abandoned himself to every distraction in order to forget them. He went everywhere, drank a great deal, bought paintings, took up construction, and above all — read.

He read, and read everything that came to hand. On coming home, while his valets were still helping him undress, he would pick up a book and start reading. From reading he passed to sleeping, from sleeping to gossip at drawing rooms and the club, from gossip to drinking and women, from drinking back to gossip, reading, and wine. Drinking became more and more both a physical and a moral necessity. Though the doctors warned him that wine was dangerous for someone of his weight, he drank heavily. He only felt fully at ease when, having mechanically poured several glasses of wine into his large mouth, he felt a pleasant warmth in his body, an amiability toward everyone, and a readiness to respond to any idea without probing it too deeply. Only after a bottle or two did he feel dimly that the terribly tangled skein of life that had previously horrified him was not as dreadful as he had thought. He was always vaguely aware of some thread of that skein, buzzing in his head after dinner or supper, while chatting, listening, or reading. But under the influence of wine he would tell himself: "It doesn't matter. I'll untangle it. I have a solution worked out, but I don't have time right now — I'll think it all through later." But the "later" never came.
In the morning, on an empty stomach, all the old questions looked as insoluble and terrible as ever, and Pierre hastily picked up a book. And if someone came to visit, he was glad.

Sometimes he recalled how he had heard that soldiers in war, when trapped under enemy fire with nothing to do, try hard to find some occupation to make it easier to bear the danger. To Pierre, all people seemed like those soldiers, seeking refuge from life: some in ambition, some in cards, some in lawmaking, some in women, some in toys, some in horses, some in politics, some in sport, some in wine, some in government affairs. "Nothing is trivial and nothing is important — it's all the same — only to escape from it as best one can," thought Pierre. "Only not to see it — that dreadful it!"
